claimBoundary: This is one provenance-bound Codex pass. It is single-model evidence, not human, instructor, independent, classroom, or multi-judge validation.

claims: Every Python value has a data type (such as int, float, or str); expressions combine values, and conversion functions move a value from one type to another.
The interpreter performs implicit type conversion to promote types automatically inside a mixed expression.
int() converts a value to an integer and removes any fractional part, so int(3.9) is 3.
True division (/) converts numbers to floats before dividing and always returns a float.
Floor division (//) computes the whole-number quotient, discarding the remainder.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §2.2 Type conversion; §2.5 Dividing integers

artifact.df: An integer-style quotient that drops any remainder.
artifact.eg: In `7 // 2`, the result is `3`, which is the whole-number quotient.
artifact.mi: It means dividing and then rounding to the nearest whole number.
artifact.cx: The operation discards the remainder rather than rounding; the related decimal-producing operator is `/`.

artifact.df: The automatic type promotion performed by the interpreter within a mixed expression.
artifact.eg: A mixed expression involving an int and a float will result in a float.
artifact.mi: Assuming the interpreter only performs explicit type changes when functions are called.
artifact.cx: Recognizing that the interpreter performs implicit type conversion to promote types automatically inside a mixed expression.

claims: Recursion solves a problem by reducing it to a simpler version of the same problem; a recursive function calls itself on a smaller input until it reaches a base case.
A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input.
The process continues until the problem is small enough that the solution is known or easily found — the base case.
Without a base case that stops the self-calls, recursion never terminates and overflows the call stack.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §12.1 Recursion basics

artifact.df: The specific state or input size that signals the end of the recursive process.
artifact.eg: In calculating the factorial of 0, the function immediately returns 1 because 0 is the base case.
artifact.mi: Thinking the termination condition is the final result of the calculation.
artifact.cx: The termination condition is the base case, which is the point where the solution is known or easily found.

artifact.df: A way to solve a problem by turning it into a smaller version of the same problem until a base case is reached.
artifact.eg: A function that counts down from 5 by calling itself with 4, then 3, then 2, until it reaches 0.
artifact.mi: Recursion just means using many loops to do the same task.
artifact.cx: A recursive solution can use self-calls on smaller inputs, while loops repeat without self-calls.

claims: A conditional statement chooses which block of code to run based on whether a condition is true; if-else takes exactly one branch, and boolean operators (and, or, not) build compound conditions.
An if statement runs its body only when the condition is true, and skips it when the condition is false.
An else clause holds statements that run when the if condition is false.
and returns True only if both conditions are true; or returns True if either is true; not inverts a single condition.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §4.2 If-else statements; §4.3 Boolean operations

artifact.df: A logic word used to combine or modify conditions.
artifact.eg: Use and to require two tests, or to accept either one, and not to flip a test.
artifact.mi: These operators are only for comparing numbers.
artifact.cx: They build compound conditions: and is true only when both parts are true, or is true when either part is true, and not reverses one condition.

artifact.df: A mechanism that dictates which set of instructions to follow based on a logical test result.
artifact.eg: Using an if statement to display a 'Pass' message if a score is 70 or higher.
artifact.mi: Thinking the program executes the code inside the if block unconditionally.
artifact.cx: An if statement runs its body only when the condition is true, and skips it when the condition is false.

claims: A for loop iterates over each element of a container — a range of numbers, a string, or a list — binding a loop variable to one element at a time.
A container can be a range of numbers, a string of characters, or a list of values.
The loop retrieves the objects of a container one at a time.
range() produces a sequence of integers and is commonly paired with a for loop to repeat the body a fixed number of times; range(n) yields 0 through n-1.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §5.2 For loop

artifact.df: A control structure that visits each item in a container one by one.
artifact.eg: Loop through a list of student names and print each name.
artifact.mi: It always means repeating a block a fixed number of times.
artifact.cx: It may also step through a string or list, not only a counted repetition.

artifact.df: The process of accessing each item within a collection sequentially.
artifact.eg: Using a for loop to process every item in a list of names.
artifact.mi: Thinking iteration means stopping after the first item is processed.
artifact.cx: Accessing each item within a collection sequentially.

claims: The rock cycle describes how Earth's three rock families — igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic — form and continually transform into one another through geologic processes.
The rock cycle describes the major Earth materials, the processes that form them, and how they relate to each other.
Igneous rock forms when liquid rock freezes solid; lithified sediment becomes sedimentary rock; pre-existing rock can transform into metamorphic rock.
If conditions melt the rocks into magma, the cycle begins anew with new igneous rocks.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §4 The rock cycle

artifact.q: When liquid rock cools and solidifies, what type of rock is produced according to the cycle?
artifact.ex: Option C is correct because igneous rock forms when liquid rock freezes solid. Option A is incorrect as metamorphic rock forms from pre-existing rock under different conditions, and Option B is incorrect as sedimentary rock forms from lithified sediment.

artifact.q: After a rock melts, the geologic cycle can start over when the molten material cools and hardens. What new rock family forms first?
artifact.ex: Igneous rock is correct because liquid rock freezes solid to form igneous rock. A plausible misconception is to choose sedimentary rock, but sedimentary rock forms when sediment is lithified, not when magma cools.

claims: Plate tectonics holds that Earth's rigid lithosphere is broken into plates that move over the ductile asthenosphere; most geologic action occurs at their three kinds of boundaries.
At divergent boundaries, lithospheric plates move away from each other and new lithosphere is created.
At convergent boundaries, two or more plates move toward each other and lithosphere is destroyed.
At a transform boundary, plates slide horizontally past each other.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §2.4 Plate boundaries

artifact.q: Where is new lithosphere generated as lithospheric plates move apart?
artifact.ex: The correct choice, Divergent boundary, is where new lithosphere is created as plates move away from each other. A plausible misconception is selecting a convergent boundary, which involves lithosphere destruction.

artifact.q: Two crustal blocks are offset along a fault, and repeated measurements show they move side by side with little change in distance between them. What boundary is indicated?
artifact.ex: Transform boundaries match lateral slipping, where plates slide horizontally past each other. The likely misconception is to confuse sideways motion with spreading or collision; those belong to divergent and convergent boundaries, respectively.

claims: Geologic time spans the roughly 4.5-billion-year history of Earth; relative dating orders events by which is older or younger, while absolute dating assigns numerical ages in years.
Absolute (numerical) dating assigns specific ages in years to mineral grains within a rock.
By the principle of superposition, in an undisturbed sequence the bottom layers are oldest and the upper layers younger.
By original horizontality, sediments and lava flows are laid down horizontally, so tilted layers were disturbed after deposition.
The Earth is about 4.54 billion years old, and this vastness of geologic time allowed life to evolve.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §7.1 Relative dating and geologic time

artifact.df: A way to place events in older-to-younger order rather than give a numerical age.
artifact.eg: A student decides which of two rock layers formed first in an outcrop.
artifact.mi: It always provides the exact number of years for a rock.
artifact.cx: Relative dating tells sequence; absolute dating gives numerical ages.

artifact.df: Assigning specific ages in years to mineral grains within a rock.
artifact.eg: Determining the exact age of a specific quartz grain in a sandstone sample.
artifact.mi: Assuming that relative dating methods can provide precise numerical ages.
artifact.cx: Absolute dating assigns specific ages in years to mineral grains within a rock.

claims: Metamorphic rock forms when heat, pressure, and fluids change a preexisting parent rock (the protolith) in the solid state, without melting it.
Metamorphism changes a solid rock's composition and texture without the mineral crystals melting.
The starting rock that undergoes metamorphism is called the parent rock, or protolith.
Directed stress aligns mineral crystals into planes, producing foliation.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §6.1 Metamorphism and metamorphic rocks

artifact.df: A change in a solid rock's composition and texture without melting.
artifact.eg: A limestone turning into marble.
artifact.mi: Melting of the rock.
artifact.cx: Changing a solid rock's composition and texture without the mineral crystals melting.

artifact.df: The original parent rock that later undergoes metamorphic change.
artifact.eg: A limestone that serves as the starting rock before metamorphism alters it.
artifact.mi: It is the mineral pattern created after metamorphism.
artifact.cx: The correction is that it names the starting rock, not the transformed one.

claims: Metamorphic rock forms when heat, pressure, and fluids change a preexisting parent rock (the protolith) in the solid state, without melting it.
Metamorphism changes a solid rock's composition and texture without the mineral crystals melting.
The starting rock that undergoes metamorphism is called the parent rock, or protolith.
Directed stress aligns mineral crystals into planes, producing foliation.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §6.1 Metamorphism and metamorphic rocks

artifact.df: The initial rock subjected to metamorphic change.
artifact.eg: Shale undergoing metamorphism.
artifact.mi: The final metamorphic rock.
artifact.cx: The starting rock that undergoes metamorphism.

artifact.df: Change in a solid rock caused by heat, pressure, and fluids without melting.
artifact.eg: A buried shale becoming a metamorphic rock while remaining solid.
artifact.mi: It requires the rock to melt first.
artifact.cx: The correction is that the mineral crystals stay solid during the change.

claims: In music theory, a scale is "any consecutive series of notes that form a progression between one note and its octave", typically by order of pitch or fundamental frequency.
A measure of the width of each scale step provides a method to classify scales.
Scales can be abstracted from performance or composition.
Therefore, any scale is distinguishable by its "step-pattern", or how its intervals interact with each other.
A specific scale is defined by its characteristic interval pattern and by a special note, known as its first degree (or tonic).
The expression scale degree refers to these numerical labels.

artifact.df: The way the intervals between consecutive notes in a scale interact.
artifact.eg: The pattern of whole and half steps in a mode.
artifact.mi: The characteristic interval pattern and the first degree.
artifact.cx: The specific scale that is defined by its characteristic interval pattern.

artifact.df: A numerical label used for notes within a scale.
artifact.eg: In a major-scale discussion, the tonic can be labeled as the first degree.
artifact.mi: It means the number of bars in the passage.
artifact.cx: It labels positions in the scale, not the length of the excerpt.

claims: In Western musical notation, the staff (UK usually stave); (plural: staves), also occasionally referred to as a pentagram, is a set of horizontal lines (usually five) with spaces between them, that each represent a different musical pitch.
Which staff positions represent which notes is determined by a clef placed at the beginning of the staff.
A clef (from French: clef 'key') is a musical symbol used to indicate which notes are represented by the lines and spaces on a musical staff.
The treble clef is also the upper staff of the grand staff used for harp and keyboard instruments.
Bass clef is the bottom clef in the grand staff for harp and keyboard instruments.

artifact.df: A symbol placed at the start of notation that shows how the staff’s lines and spaces should be read.
artifact.eg: A treble clef at the beginning of a staff tells the reader which pitches the upper lines and spaces represent.
artifact.mi: It names a single note for the whole piece.
artifact.cx: It does not label one note; it indicates how notes on the staff are represented.

artifact.df: The set of horizontal lines (usually five) with spaces between them that each represent a different musical pitch.
artifact.eg: The staff is a set of horizontal lines with spaces between them.
artifact.mi: The staff is a set of horizontal lines (usually five) with spaces between them, that each represent a different musical pitch. Correction: The staff is a set of horizontal lines (usually five) with spaces between them, that each represent a different musical pitch.
artifact.cx: A set of horizontal lines (usually five) with spaces between them, that each represent a different musical pitch.

claims: In music, harmony is the concept of combining different sounds in order to create new, distinct musical ideas.
In these genres, chord progressions are the defining feature on which melody and rhythm are built.
Chord progressions are the foundation of harmony in Western musical tradition from the common practice era of classical music to the 21st century.
A first chord forms a 'progression' with a second chord, and a second with a third.
For example, the relative minor of C major is A minor, and in the key of A minor, the i, iv and v chords are A minor, D minor and E minor.
In many styles of popular and traditional music, chord progressions are expressed using the name and "quality" of the chords.

artifact.df: A sequence in which one chord moves to another and then onward.
artifact.eg: In A minor, i–iv–v can be A minor, D minor, and E minor.
artifact.mi: A progression is just a list of unrelated chords.
artifact.cx: The chords are connected in order, and that ordered motion is what makes them a progression.

artifact.df: A sequence of chords that forms the basis of harmony.
artifact.eg: A first chord forming a 'progression' with a second chord.
artifact.mi: Misconception: Believing that chord progressions are only used in popular music. Correction: Chord progressions are the foundation of harmony in Western musical tradition from the common practice era of classical music to the 21st century (Claim 2).
artifact.cx: A first chord forming a 'progression' with a second chord.

claims: In Western musical notation, the staff (UK usually stave); (plural: staves), also occasionally referred to as a pentagram, is a set of horizontal lines (usually five) with spaces between them, that each represent a different musical pitch.
Which staff positions represent which notes is determined by a clef placed at the beginning of the staff.
A clef (from French: clef 'key') is a musical symbol used to indicate which notes are represented by the lines and spaces on a musical staff.
The treble clef is also the upper staff of the grand staff used for harp and keyboard instruments.
Bass clef is the bottom clef in the grand staff for harp and keyboard instruments.

artifact.df: A set of horizontal lines with spaces that represent different pitches.
artifact.eg: On a piano lead sheet, the five-line staff places notes in different vertical positions to show pitch.
artifact.mi: It is just a blank grid for note spacing.
artifact.cx: Its lines and spaces correspond to different musical pitches.

artifact.df: A set of horizontal lines with spaces on which musical pitches are represented.
artifact.eg: The five horizontal lines and spaces on which notes are written.
artifact.mi: A single musical pitch.
artifact.cx: The staff is the set of lines and spaces, not a single pitch.

claims: A UX research plan turns a decision need into actionable learning objectives, participants, tasks, evidence-capture roles, and a rehearsal-ready study setup.
The team should agree what it wants to learn from the research round before selecting study details.
A prototype used in research should work end-to-end and be usable and accessible in the research venue.
Researchers should run through test tasks on the day before the research session.
A practice session with a team member can expose procedure problems before participants arrive.

artifact.df: Specific things the team wants the study to clarify so the findings can support a decision.
artifact.eg: A team wants to learn whether shoppers can compare shipping options before choosing a plan.
artifact.mi: The team should start by writing every possible research question.
artifact.cx: Begin with the decision need, then turn it into focused objectives.

artifact.df: Specific goals derived from a decision need that guide the research.
artifact.eg: Defining the objective as 'Understand user flow for checkout' instead of 'Study the checkout process'.
artifact.mi: Believing objectives are simply broad topics to cover.
artifact.cx: Objectives must be actionable, turning a need into specific learning goals.

The team should agree what it wants to learn from the research round before selecting study details.

artifact.mi: It is the same as testing with real participants.
artifact.cx: It helps expose procedure problems early, but it is not a substitute for participant sessions.

artifact.df: A practice run conducted with a team member to identify procedural issues before participants arrive.
artifact.eg: Running through test tasks with a team member the day before the research session.
artifact.mi: Assuming participants will perform tasks perfectly on the day.
artifact.cx: A practice session with a team member can expose procedure problems before participants arrive. [3, 4]
